cast.name: Sherlock Holmes
aliases: the old man by the brazier
cast.note: Consulting detective of 221B Baker Street, narrated through Watson's eyes; present throughout the cases in these divisions and the one who solves each.

cast.name: Dr. Watson
cast.note: Narrator and Holmes's companion, a doctor; first-person voice throughout these divisions.

cast.name: Wilhelm Gottsreich Sigismond von Ormstein
cast.note: Hereditary King of Bohemia who visits Baker Street disguised as Count Von Kramm to recover his photograph with Irene Adler; distinct from the Bohemian royal figures of other stories.

cast.name: Irene Adler
cast.note: Former opera contralto and adventuress of Briony Lodge who marries Godfrey Norton and flees to the Continent.

cast.name: Godfrey Norton
cast.note: Barrister of the Inner Temple who visits Irene Adler and becomes her husband; not to be confused with other Norton-named figures.

cast.name: John
cast.note: Irene Adler's coachman sent to watch Holmes; distinct from the cabman and stable-boy John of the Man With the Twisted Lip.

cast.name: Mrs. Turner
cast.note: Landlady at Baker Street; distinct from Mrs. Hudson, the landlady of other stories.

cast.name: Mary Jane
cast.note: Watson's careless servant mentioned in passing by Holmes's deductions; distinct from the other Mary characters.

cast.name: the elderly woman
cast.note: Elderly servant at Briony Lodge who tells Holmes the lady has left for the Continent.

cast.name: the loungers
cast.note: Group of confederates staging the street quarrel and false fire alarm on Holmes's orders.

cast.name: the slim youth in an ulster
cast.note: Unidentified youth who greets Holmes by name in the street at the end of the Bohemia story.

cast.name: Jabez Wilson
cast.note: Stout, red-haired pawnbroker of Saxe-Coburg Square who brings the Red-Headed League case.

cast.name: Vincent Spaulding
cast.note: Clean-shaven assistant of Wilson who is really John Clay's accomplice in disguise; distinct from the criminal leader Clay.

cast.name: Duncan Ross
cast.note: Small red-headed man running the League office at Pope's Court under a false identity, allied with Clay.

cast.name: John Clay
cast.note: Royal-blooded young thief and forger who tunnelled from the pawnshop cellar to the bank; arrested in the vault.

cast.name: Archie
cast.note: Red-haired accomplice of John Clay who escapes down the hole.

cast.name: Peter Jones
cast.note: Official police agent from Scotland Yard who hunts with Holmes in the Red-Headed League case.

cast.name: Mr. Merryweather
cast.note: Solemn chairman of the bank directors of the City and Suburban Bank branch, and a whist player.

cast.name: Miss Mary Sutherland
cast.note: Typewriting young woman whose missing fiancé Hosmer Angel is her stepfather in disguise; distinct from the Mary of other stories, and the Miss Sutherland mentioned in Red-Headed League only in passing.

cast.name: Ezekiah Hopkins
cast.note: Deceased American millionaire who founded the Red-Headed League; referred to only.

cast.name: Mr. James Windibank
cast.note: Mary Sutherland's stepfather who secretly disguised himself as her fiancé Hosmer Angel to prevent the marriage; Hosmer Angel is not a real person in the story.

cast.name: Mrs. Sutherland
cast.note: Widow who remarried Windibank and was in on the deception; not on stage.

cast.name: Mr. Hardy
cast.note: Former foreman of Mary's late father's business; mentioned only.

cast.name: Mrs. Watson
cast.note: Watson's wife, appearing only at the opening of The Man With the Twisted Lip and in the Boscombe breakfast scene.

cast.name: Lestrade
cast.note: Ferret-like Scotland Yard detective; appears in the Boscombe and Noble Bachelor cases.

cast.name: Alice Turner
cast.note: Daughter of John Turner who hires Holmes in the Boscombe Valley case; distinct from Alice the maid of the Noble Bachelor case.

cast.name: James McCarthy
cast.note: Son of Charles McCarthy, accused of killing his father in the Boscombe Valley case.

cast.name: Charles McCarthy
cast.note: Former convict driver, tenant of Hatherley Farm, and murder victim by the pool.

cast.name: John Turner
cast.note: Wealthy landowner of the Hall and the actual killer in the Boscombe Valley case.

cast.name: William Crowder
cast.note: Game-keeper employed by Turner who witnessed McCarthy walking alone.

cast.name: Patience Moran
cast.note: Fourteen-year-old daughter of the lodge-keeper who saw the McCarthys quarrelling.

cast.name: Dr. Willows
cast.note: Physician attending John Turner.

cast.name: John Cobb
cast.note: Groom and servant of McCarthy; mentioned only.

cast.name: Moran, the lodge-keeper
cast.note: Lodge-keeper of the Boscombe Valley estate, father of Patience Moran.

cast.name: the barmaid
cast.note: Bristol barmaid whom James secretly married; mentioned only.

cast.name: John Openshaw
cast.note: Young client, nephew of Colonel Elias Openshaw, found drowned near Waterloo Bridge; not to be confused with his uncle.

cast.name: Colonel Elias Openshaw
cast.note: Uncle of John Openshaw, former Confederate colonel who dies in a garden pool after the K.K.K. warning; not to be confused with John.

cast.name: Joseph Openshaw
cast.note: Brother of Colonel Elias and father of John; dies falling into a chalk-pit.

cast.name: Major Prendergast
cast.note: Army officer who referred Openshaw to Holmes; mentioned only.

cast.name: Mr. Fordham
cast.note: Horsham lawyer who witnessed the colonel's will; mentioned only.

cast.name: Major Freebody
cast.note: Commander of a fort on Portsdown Hill; mentioned only.

cast.name: Captain James Calhoun
cast.note: Master of the barque Lone Star and leader of the K.K.K. gang; never on stage.

cast.name: Police-Constable Cook
cast.note: H Division constable who heard the cry near Waterloo Bridge; mentioned only.

cast.name: Hudson
cast.note: Name in the colonel's 1869 diary page; mentioned only.

cast.name: McCauley
cast.note: Name in the 1869 diary page; mentioned only.

cast.name: Paramore
cast.note: Name in the 1869 diary page; mentioned only.

cast.name: John Swain
cast.note: Name in the 1869 diary page; mentioned only.

cast.name: Mary
cast.note: Household servant at Horsham; mentioned only.

cast.name: Isa Whitney
cast.note: Brother of Elias Whitney and opium addict found in an opium den; husband of Kate Whitney.

cast.name: Kate Whitney
cast.note: Wife of Isa Whitney who comes to Watson's house asking for help.

cast.name: Malay attendant
cast.note: Attendant at the opium den who offers Watson a pipe.

cast.name: Lascar manager
cast.note: Keeper of the opium den in Upper Swandam Lane.

cast.name: Dane assistant
cast.note: Assistant at the opium den; mentioned only.

cast.name: Neville St. Clair
aliases: the beggar with the twisted lip
cast.note: Respectable Lee gentleman who disguised himself as the beggar Hugh Boone; Hugh Boone is the same person and is merged here.

cast.name: Mrs. St. Clair
cast.note: Wife of Neville St. Clair living at The Cedars in Lee.

cast.name: Inspector Barton
cast.note: Police inspector who searched the den; mentioned only.

cast.name: Inspector Bradstreet
cast.note: Police inspector who receives Holmes at Bow Street in one story and arrests Horner in another.

cast.name: John the cabman
cast.note: Cabman who drives Whitney home and stable-boy at The Cedars; distinct from John Coachman of the Bohemia story.

cast.name: the horse
cast.note: Reference point for the conveyance rather than a character.

cast.name: Victor Hatherley
cast.note: Young hydraulic engineer who brings his ordeal to Watson and Holmes; the Hatherley of the title.

cast.name: Colonel Lysander Stark
cast.note: Thin German-accented coiner who hires Hatherley under false pretences.

cast.name: Elise
cast.note: Young woman apparently Stark's wife or companion who warns Hatherley.

cast.name: Mr. Ferguson
cast.note: Stark's secretary and manager who helps carry Hatherley away.

cast.name: Jeremiah Hayling
aliases: the missing engineer named in the advertisement
cast.note: Earlier victim of Stark's press, not present on stage.

cast.name: The guard
cast.note: Railway guard who brings Hatherley to Watson at dawn.

cast.name: The maid
cast.note: Watson's maid who announces visitors; unnamed.

cast.name: The station-master
cast.note: Station-master at Eyford who reports the fire.

cast.name: The porter
cast.note: Night porter at Eyford Station.

cast.name: The driver
cast.note: Unnamed driver who takes Hatherley from Eyford; never seen.

cast.name: Lord Robert St. Simon
cast.note: Aristocratic bridegroom deserted at the wedding breakfast.

cast.name: Hatty Doran
cast.note: Bride who vanished at the wedding breakfast to run off with her first husband Frank Moulton.

cast.name: Francis Hay Moulton
cast.note: Hatty's first husband, presumed dead, who appears at the wedding.

cast.name: Flora Millar
aliases: the woman who caused the disturbance
cast.note: Former dancer and mistress of Lord St. Simon; distinct from Frank Moulton despite shared initials.

cast.name: Alice
cast.note: Hatty Doran's American maid from California; distinct from Alice Turner of Boscombe Valley.

cast.name: Aloysius Doran
cast.note: Rich San Francisco mining man and father of Hatty Doran.

cast.name: Duke of Balmoral
cast.note: Father of Lord St. Simon; absent from the action.

cast.name: Lord Backwater
cast.note: Acquaintance who recommended Holmes; absent.

cast.name: Alexander Holder
cast.note: Senior partner of the banking firm Holder & Stevenson whose coronet is stolen.

cast.name: Arthur Holder
cast.note: Son of Alexander Holder suspected of stealing the coronet; innocent.

cast.name: Mary Holder
cast.note: Niece of Alexander Holder who secretly took the coronet to her lover; distinct from Mary Sutherland and Mary Jane.

cast.name: Sir George Burnwell
cast.note: Aristocratic gambler, Mary's lover, who took three beryls from the coronet.

cast.name: The illustrious client
cast.note: Unnamed high-ranking person who deposited the coronet; off-stage.

cast.name: Lucy Parr
cast.note: Second waiting-maid at Fairbank with a sweetheart.

cast.name: Francis Prosper
cast.note: Greengrocer with a wooden leg, Lucy Parr's sweetheart.

cast.name: The receiver
cast.note: Dealer who bought the stolen beryls; off-stage.

cast.name: Henry Baker
cast.note: Grizzled gentleman who lost the hat and goose; member of the Alpha Inn goose club.

cast.name: Peterson
cast.note: Honest commissionaire who finds the hat and goose.

cast.name: John Horner
cast.note: Plumber wrongly accused of stealing the blue carbuncle.

cast.name: Countess of Morcar
cast.note: Owner of the blue carbuncle.

cast.name: James Ryder
cast.note: Head attendant at the Hotel Cosmopolitan who stole the stone and hid it in a goose.

cast.name: Catherine Cusack
cast.note: Maid to the Countess who was Ryder's accomplice.

cast.name: Breckinridge
cast.note: Covent Garden poultry salesman who sold the geese.

cast.name: Windigate
cast.note: Landlord of the Alpha Inn and host of the goose club.

cast.name: Mrs. Oakshott
cast.note: Poultry supplier at Brixton Road and Ryder's sister.

cast.name: Mrs. Hudson
cast.note: Holmes's landlady; mentioned only.

cast.name: Maudsley
cast.note: Ryder's former associate; mentioned only.

cast.name: the goose
aliases: the white goose with a barred tail
cast.note: White goose that swallowed the stone.

cast.name: Helen Stoner
cast.note: Young woman who consults Holmes about her dead twin's death at Stoke Moran.

cast.name: Julia Stoner
cast.note: Helen's twin sister who died at Stoke Moran.

cast.name: Dr. Grimesby Roylott
cast.note: Violent Stoke Moran physician, stepfather of Helen and Julia, who dies of the swamp adder.

cast.name: Percy Armitage
cast.note: Helen's intended husband; mentioned only.

cast.name: Miss Honoria Westphail
cast.note: Maternal aunt of Helen and Julia; mentioned only.

cast.name: Mrs. Farintosh
cast.note: Earlier client of Holmes; mentioned only.

cast.name: Swamp adder
cast.note: Deadly snake that kills Roylott.

cast.name: Cheetah and baboon
cast.note: Animals kept by Roylott; heard and glimpsed at night.

cast.name: Violet Hunter
cast.note: Governess who consults Holmes and is taken to Copper Beeches.

cast.name: Jephro Rucastle
cast.note: Stout father of Alice Rucastle who imprisons his daughter and is mauled by his mastiff.

cast.name: Mrs. Rucastle
cast.note: Pale second wife of Jephro Rucastle.

cast.name: Edward
cast.note: Six-year-old spoiled son of the Rucastles.

cast.name: Alice Rucastle
cast.note: Daughter of Jephro Rucastle by his first wife, held in the barricaded room; distinct from Alice Turner and Alice the maid.

cast.name: Toller
cast.note: Drunken groom at Copper Beeches who lets the mastiff loose.

cast.name: Mrs. Toller
cast.note: Gaunt wife of Toller and cook at Copper Beeches.

cast.name: Mr. Fowler
cast.note: Alice Rucastle's fiancé who watched the house; not on stage.

cast.name: Miss Stoper
cast.note: Manageress of the Westaway governess agency.

cast.name: Carlo
cast.note: Giant mastiff at Copper Beeches, shot by Watson.

cast.name: The police inspector
cast.note: Police inspector who arrests Arthur and conducts the search at Fairbank; not named.

a-scandal-in-bohemia.tone: Brisk, witty Victorian detective mystery with a touch of comedy at Holmes's expense and a sense of royal danger tempered by fond irony.
depiction_rules: Holmes is shown with his analytical, observant manner and disguises (groom, clergyman) rendered convincingly; no cocaine use should be shown explicitly.
The King is shown masked in his first appearance, unmasked only after he tears the mask off in the room.
Irene Adler is glimpsed rather than fully revealed in the early sections, presented as beautiful and resolute; her face is seen clearly only at the threshold and in the photograph.
The street quarrel and smoke-rocket fire alarm are shown as staged comedy, not real violence; Holmes's blood is red paint.

era.name: London and Bohemia, late 1880s (March 1888)
era.people: English gentlemen in frock and tweed; a Bohemian King of Teutonic bearing; London street types such as cabmen, ostlers, a scissors-grinder, guardsmen and loungers; servants in plain dress.
era.dress: Victorian: frock coats, top hats, ulsters, walking dress and bonnets for women; the King wears rich astrakhan-trimmed double-breasted coat, a blue cloak lined with flame-coloured silk and a beryl brooch, with fur-trimmed boots.
era.buildings_and_objects: Gaslit London with lamplighting at dusk; hansom cabs, broughams and landaus drawn by horses; villas with sliding panels and window fasteners; cabinet-size photographs; pink notepaper watermarked with Bohemian paper-mill marks; a gasogene and spirit case.
era.technology: Pre-electric lighting (gas and oil lamps), railway travel (the 5:15 train from Charing Cross), telegraph wires, smoke-rockets and plumber's tools; no telephones or motor cars in use here.

the-red-headed-league.tone: Dry, comic, foggy Victorian mystery: a whimsical premise giving way to tense darkness underground, with Holmes's quiet confidence.
depiction_rules: Show Wilson's flaming red hair plainly, as it is the plot's key feature.
Show Spaulding's disguise and Clay's refined manner without over-explaining the concealment.
Keep the vault scenes dim, lantern-lit, and mostly in shadow to preserve suspense.
Depict the crowd at Pope's Court as a jostling mass of varied red hair shades, not individuals.

era.name: London, autumn 1890
era.people: Late-Victorian Londoners: tradesmen, clerks, pawnbrokers, bankers, police agents, with a crowd of red-haired applicants from all over the city.
era.dress: Frock-coats, top-hats, waistcoats with watch chains, greatcoats, bowler hats (derbies), and working-class caps and shawls for the crowd.
era.buildings_and_objects: Gas-lit streets, brick townhouses, shopfronts with gilt balls, the City's counting-houses, cellars with lead-foiled crates of napoleons, stone floors and iron gates.
era.technology: Hansom cabs, the Underground railway, handheld cameras, lanterns and dark lanterns, revolvers; no electric lighting or telephones.

a-case-of-identity.tone: Quiet, domestic Victorian detective mystery with an undercurrent of comic deceit and sly irony rather than menace.
depiction_rules: Holmes is tall, thin, sharp-featured, in a dressing gown or shirt-sleeves in his rooms, with a clay pipe and the gaunt air of a man absorbed in thought.
Watson is a stout-to-average, mustachioed doctor in a frock-coat, seen mostly as an attentive observer.
Mary Sutherland is a broad-faced, good-humoured young woman in a large feathered hat, fur boa and brown dress with purple plush trim; she should look nervous but simple-hearted.
Windibank in disguise (as Angel) wears tinted glasses, bushy black side-whiskers and moustache; unmasked he is clean-shaven, sallow and sharp-eyed.
Do not depict the disguise as anything more than a costume; the fraud is a domestic trick, not violence.
The wedding-day cab and church need only be suggested in the reading room; avoid gore or alarm.

era.name: London, 1880s, late Victorian
era.people: Londoners of the lower middle class: typewriters, clerks, plumbers, wine travellers, cab drivers; women of modest means in wide-brimmed hats and bustles.
era.dress: Frock-coats, top-hats, high collars and tinted spectacles for men; broad-brimmed feathered hats, fur boas, jet-bead jackets and plush-trimmed dresses for women.
era.buildings_and_objects: Gaslit Baker Street rooms with a coal fire, hansom cabs and four-wheelers, a St. Saviour's-style church near King's Cross, Leadenhall Street offices, Post Office poste restante, printed newspaper advertisements, chemical glassware and test-tubes.
era.technology: Typewriters exist and are a new novelty in offices; telegrams and the post are current; no telephone, electric light, or motorcars.

the-boscombe-valley-mystery.tone: Cool, misty English countryside melancholy with a tense detective's focus; tragic and quiet rather than lurid, with the sense of a hidden past surfacing.
depiction_rules: Show the murder victim only as a body or unseen; do not depict the blows or the bloodied head in graphic detail.
Holmes is lean and gaunt in a grey travelling cloak and cloth cap; keep him in the tradition of Sidney Paget's illustrations.
Show the damp meadow, reed-fringed pool, beech tree and footprints as clues rather than as spectacle.
Do not depict John Turner's confession as a dramatic flashback; keep him seated and weary in the hotel room.
Avoid romanticising Turner's Ballarat past; render the gold-convoy robbery only as memory, if at all.

era.name: England and Australia in the 1880s, Victorian era
era.people: English country folk, farmers, gamekeepers and gentry in Herefordshire; former gold-diggers and convicts from Victoria, Australia, now settled as landowners and tenants.
era.dress: Victorian tweed suits, long travelling cloaks, dustcoats and leather leggings for the country; the gentry in frock coats; women in dark dresses; Holmes in a grey cloak and cloth cap.
era.buildings_and_objects: Stone and slate farmhouses with lichen-covered walls, a country hotel with a yellow-backed novel and sofa, a lodge, a red-pinnacled Hall, and an 1880s rail network.
era.technology: Railways, telegrams and newspapers exist; no telephones or photography at the scene. Forensic work is done by eye, lens and cigar-ash identification.

the-five-orange-pips.tone: Stormy, foreboding and claustrophobic in London, with dread growing from the quiet Horsham household into a grim, fatal hunt at sea.
depiction_rules: Show the K.K.K. warnings only as the small dried orange pips and the scrawled letters, never as hooded figures or lynching scenes.
Do not depict the colonel's death or the chalk-pit fall in gory detail; keep them off-screen or suggested by the pool and the empty box.
Holmes is shown in his Baker Street rooms with pipe, violin and reference books, not in disguise.
Keep the American slavery and Reconstruction background as referenced politics, with no graphic racial violence shown.
Show the Lone Star only at a distance or as a final shattered stern-post, not a lingering shipboard scene.

era.name: Victorian England, 1883 to 1885, with American Reconstruction and Confederate backdrop
era.people: English professionals, servants and police in London and Sussex; Openshaw is a young English gentleman; the colonel is a former Southern planter, and the gang are American sailors of Finnish and German crews.
era.dress: Frock coats, waistcoats and overcoats for men, long waterproof coats and umbrellas in rain; pince-nez for John; plain dress for servants and dock workers.
era.buildings_and_objects: Gaslit Baker Street sitting room with fire and lamp, Horsham country house with attic lumber-room and garden sundial, brass cash-box, chalk-pits, Waterloo Bridge, Albert Dock and sailing barques.
era.technology: Gas lighting, railways and telegraph, steamboats and sailing ships, printed newspapers and encyclopaedias; no telephones, motorcars or electric light.

the-man-with-the-twisted-lip.tone: A wry, late-Victorian mystery of London fog and gaslight, with moments of comic reversal and a melancholy undertone of addiction.
depiction_rules: Show the opium den as squalid and dim, with bodies in berths and small red pipe-glows; do not depict drug use in graphic or glamorised detail.
Neville St. Clair's disguise as Hugh Boone should be shown with the scar, twisted lip and red hair in the street scenes, and its removal in the cell scene.
Holmes's disguise as an old opium smoker is a costume to be shown convincingly aged, not as a real addict.
The Thames, the wharves and the murky river should carry the atmosphere; avoid depicting any body in the water.

era.name: London and Kent, June 1889
era.people: Late-Victorian Londoners and Kentish villagers; dock labourers, Lascar and Malay seamen in the East End, respectable middle-class families in Lee.
era.dress: Frock coats, waistcoats, top hats and bowler hats for gentlemen; high-necked dresses, mousseline and pinafores for women; constables in frogged jackets and peaked caps; ragged beggar's clothes for Boone.
era.buildings_and_objects: Gas and oil street lamps, cobbled and gravel streets, stone wharves and bridges over the Thames, opium dens with wooden berths, hansom cabs and dog-carts, villas in gardens, the Bow Street police station with its whitewashed cells.
era.technology: Horse-drawn transport and railways, telegrams, and the telephone; no motor cars, electric lighting or photography beyond early plates in the police files.

the-adventure-of-the-blue-carbuncle.tone: Wintry Christmas-season mystery: cold streets, warm firelit rooms, dry humour and a moral undertone of mercy.
depiction_rules: Holmes and Watson are shown in Victorian dress; Holmes in his purple dressing-gown or ulster at home and out of doors.
The blue carbuncle is a small, intensely brilliant blue stone, shown as a point of light, not a large gem.
The goose is a plain white bird with a black bar across the tail; no gore in the scenes with the goose.
Ryder's confession and near-collapse may show distress but no violence beyond his fall into the rug.
Holmes's deductions from the hat are shown as scrutiny with a lens, not as spectacle.

era.name: London, late Victorian, the days after Christmas
era.people: Londoners of all classes: a commissionaire, a plumber, a salesman, a publican, a hotel attendant, and gentlemen in frock-coats and Scotch bonnets.
era.dress: Heavy wool ulsters, cravats, top hats, bowler and billycock hats, frock-coats, aprons for tradesmen, long skirts for women.
era.buildings_and_objects: Gaslit streets and shops, fanlights over doors, public houses with private bars, Covent Garden stalls under hanging lamps, a four-wheeler cab, clay pipes, basket-chairs, a strong-box.
era.technology: Gas lighting and coal fires; newspapers and advertisements in evening papers; no electric lighting except as a simile; no telephone; hansom and four-wheeled cabs.

the-adventure-of-the-speckled-band.tone: Gothic and foreboding, with rural Surrey spring light giving way to a claustrophobic, dread-filled night at a decaying manor.
depiction_rules: The snake may be shown only in the final scene and kept at a distance; no gore on Roylott's body beyond stillness and the coiled serpent.
Roylott should be drawn as a huge, looming, bird-of-prey figure with yellow, weathered face and burning eyes, not as a cartoon villain.
The speckled band reads as a yellow headband with brown speckles, which is the reveal; do not show it early.
Holmes and Watson should appear in period dress as gentlemen; Watson is never the dominant figure.
Keep the nocturnal scenes dark and lit only by lamp or dark-lantern light; avoid showing the cheetah and baboon clearly.

era.name: Surrey, England, 1883
era.people: English gentry and rural villagers; a Saxon-descended landowning family in decline; gipsies camping on family land; a metropolitan London professional class.
era.dress: Victorian: women in dark mourning dresses, veils and bonnets; men in frock coats, top hats, high gaiters; Roylott in a long grey dressing-gown and red Turkish slippers.
era.buildings_and_objects: Grey lichen-stained stone manor with a high central block and curving wings, one wing ruined and boarded; whitewashed corridors, worm-eaten oak panelling, iron-barred shutters, iron safe, oil lamps and dark-lanterns, a trap and dog-cart.
era.technology: Railways connect Leatherhead and Waterloo; telegraph-era communication; no electric light, no telephone, and no modern forensic chemical tests for snake venom.

the-adventure-of-the-engineers-thumb.tone: Tense, claustrophobic Victorian mystery: a clammy, secretive country house, rising dread in the press scene, and dry, wry detection in London.
depiction_rules: Show the hydraulic press's descending ceiling as a threat but do not depict the mutilation graphically; the bandaged bloodied hand may be shown restrained.
Holmes is shown in his dressing-gown and armchair, smoking, with heavy-lidded composure.
Stark should be drawn gaunt and sharp-faced, with a bright, suspicious gaze.
Elise appears only at the doorway and window, beautiful and frightened, never fully revealed as a villain.
No modern machinery; the press is wooden-walled with an iron floor and water cylinders.

era.name: Late Victorian England, summer 1889
era.people: English professionals and tradesmen; a German-speaking foreign couple and an Englishman in Berkshire country houses; railway officials and Scotland Yard inspectors.
era.dress: Frock coats, waistcoats, tweed suits and caps for men; dark rich gowns for women; Holmes in a dressing-gown at home.
era.buildings_and_objects: Terraced London townhouses with consulting-rooms, Baker Street lodgings, gas-lit and oil-lamp-lit rooms, a dilapidated country house with bare upper floors, whitewashed walls, and a small rural station.
era.technology: Steam railways and hansom cabs, hydraulic presses, oil lamps and candles, ordnance maps and compasses; no telephone in the story, no electric light, no motor car.

the-adventure-of-the-noble-bachelor.tone: Urbane Victorian detective mystery with a wry, faintly comic undertone and domestic intimacy in the Baker Street rooms.
depiction_rules: Show Holmes and Watson in the Baker Street rooms in Victorian dress, with fire, papers, and the supper laid out.
Lord St. Simon is a fastidious aristocrat: high collar, frock-coat, yellow gloves, golden eyeglasses on a cord.
Hatty Doran should be shown with lustrous dark hair and a striking face, consistent with the ivory miniature.
Do not show the bride's flight or the Serpentine search as violent; keep the mood civil and sly.
Avoid depicting the Apache attack in detail; Frank's past is told only in speech.

era.name: Victorian London, c. 1888-1890s, with American Western backstory (California, Montana, Arizona, New Mexico)
era.people: English aristocrats, Scotland Yard officers, and London servants; Americans from San Francisco and mining camps of the Rockies and the Pacific slope, rugged and sunburnt.
era.dress: Frock-coats, high collars, top hats, ulsters and bonnets for women, wedding silk and satin with veil and wreath; policemen in pea-jacket and cravat for Lestrade.
era.buildings_and_objects: Gas-lit Baker Street lodgings with mahogany table and basket-chair, Hanover Square church, Lancaster Gate townhouse, Hyde Park and the Serpentine, Northumberland Avenue hotel, cards, newspapers, and cigars.
era.technology: Newspapers and printed society columns, hansom cabs, handwritten letters with quill pens, pencil notes; no telephone or photography beyond the miniature and cartes.

the-adventure-of-the-beryl-coronet.tone: Winter gloom and a tense, quietly intense domestic crisis, with the cold February light and snowy streets underscoring grief, suspicion, and a slow return to hope.
depiction_rules: Show Holmes as lean, sharp-eyed and dressing-gowned indoors; disguised as a shabby loafer in a worn coat and cravat when out.
Do not show the coronet's ruined gold corner in close, gory detail; the stolen beryls are gems in a triangular gold piece.
Sir George Burnwell's identity is revealed late; he may be shown only obliquely (boots, figure in the lane) before the explanation.
Arthur appears barefoot in shirt and trousers during the night scene; keep the mood restrained rather than melodramatic.
Mary is pale and dark-haired, with a composed, self-restrained bearing.

era.name: Late Victorian London and Streatham, c. 1880s
era.people: Upper-middle-class London bankers and their families, aristocratic gamblers, servants and tradesmen, and a crowd of City clerks and cabmen.
era.dress: Frock-coats, shining top hats, gaiters and pearl-grey trousers for gentlemen; dark-coloured dresses and shawls for ladies; servants in plain uniforms; Holmes's disguise of a worn coat and red cravat.
era.buildings_and_objects: Brick and white-stone townhouses, a bow-window in Baker Street, a bank with private safes and bureaus, gas lighting, an iron-gated carriage drive, a lumber-room cupboard, and a jeweller's coronet of thirty-nine beryls.
era.technology: Gas lamps and the Metropolitan underground railway; hansom cabs; no telephone; handwritten notes and cheques; magnifying lenses and plaster-of-paris-era detection; no electric light.

the-adventure-of-the-copper-beeches.tone: Quiet, foggy domestic unease in London giving way to a sunny but menacing Hampshire countryside, ending in a sudden violent climax; restrained Victorian detective mood rather than gothic excess.
depiction_rules: Show the mastiff's attack only at the end, and keep Rucastle's wounds offstage or lightly suggested rather than graphic.
Do not depict Alice Rucastle's imprisonment in detail; the barricaded room may be shown empty or dim with the bed and linen.
Violet's cut hair may be shown as short and the electric-blue dress as worn but well-fitted.
Holmes is shown in his Baker Street manner with pipe and dressing-gown contexts as appropriate; avoid anachronistic gadgets.
Show the copper beeches as a dark-leafed group of trees before a whitewashed house.

era.name: Late Victorian England, c. 1890s, Hampshire countryside and London
era.people: English middle and working classes: a governess, a stout gentleman, a drunken groom and his wife, a sad young wife and a spoiled child.
era.dress: Victorian day wear: governess's plain neat dress, a cloak and hat, a gentleman's suit with a waistcoat, Violet's electric-blue dress of beige-toned material, working-class servants' plain clothing.
era.buildings_and_objects: Baker Street sitting-room with gas lighting and a coal fire; a whitewashed country house with a drawing-room and long windows; outbuildings and an iron bed used as a barricade; old inns and a cathedral town of Winchester.
era.technology: Telegraph and telegrams, railway trains with timetables (Bradshaw), gas lamps, dog-carts and traps; no motor cars, no telephones at the house, no electric lighting.

brief.tone: Brisk, foggy Victorian detective mood: witty and comic at its lighter edges, tense and gothic in its darker stretches, always with dry restraint and gaslit intimacy.
depiction_rules: Holmes is lean and sharp-eyed, in dressing-gown or ulster, with pipe and violin; disguises are convincing costumes, never real addiction.
Violence, wounds and deaths are kept offstage, restrained, or suggested by objects rather than shown in gore.
Opium dens and drug use are squalid and dim, never glamorised.
Holmes's cocaine use is never shown explicitly.
Dim, lamp-lit or dark-lantern light for night and vault scenes to preserve suspense.
Avoid anachronistic gadgets, telephones, electric light and motor cars in any scene.

eras.name: Victorian England, 1880s to early 1890s
eras.people: Londoners of every class: gentlemen, clerks, tradesmen, cabmen, servants and police, with country gentry and farm folk in the provinces.
eras.dress: Frock-coats, top hats, bowler hats, ulsters and tweeds for men; bonnets, bustles, high-necked and plush-trimmed dresses for women; plain dress for servants and labourers.
eras.buildings_and_objects: Gaslit streets and rooms with coal or oil lamps, hansom cabs and dog-carts, brick townhouses, country manors and farmhouses, printed newspapers, handwritten letters and telegrams, clay pipes and cigars.
eras.technology: Railways, telegraph and telegrams, the early Underground, typewriters as a novelty and early photography; no telephones in the story's main scenes, no electric light, no motor cars.
